issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: 'Being followed or tracked' is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one and with the rest of the profile, which centers on grief, guilt, and generalized somatic alarm rather than a pursuit/persecution context. It stands apart from the other trigger items and does not connect plausibly to the memory content provided.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy' is not well aligned with the rest of the formulation and item set. The profile otherwise emphasizes guilt, grief, misery, fragmented/numb recall, and bodily false alarms after a loved-one trauma. A 'going crazy' appraisal is possible, but here it appears weakly supported by the trigger and memory content and feels clinically out of step relative to the otherwise bereavement/guilt-focused presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, severe guilt, misery, and a sense that life has been destroyed can be coherent. However, the specific appraisal 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is notably more global and suicidal in tone than the rest of the selected profile, and it is not supported by corresponding threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content. With the provided five components, this item stands out as insufficiently anchored to the rest of the formulation-relevant material, making the node less internally coherent.

vignette: Kaikea had always been a bright and cheerful young man, loved by his friends and family for his warm smile and infectious laugh. But all of that changed on the day his younger brother, Mana, died in a tragic car accident. Kaikea was 22 at the time, and his world was shattered. Mana's funeral was a blur of pain and grief for Kaikea. He remembered feeling numb as he walked through the crowded church, surrounded by the mournful faces of their friends and family. But one moment stood out to him - when he caught a whiff of the priest's cologne, which smelled eerily similar to his brother's favorite scent. The smell hit him like a punch to the gut, transporting him back to memories of Mana. In the months that followed, Kaikea found himself becoming increasingly withdrawn. He couldn't bear the thought of going to funerals or visiting cemeteries - the mere mention of it made him feel queasy. He began to avoid social gatherings, fearing he would encounter someone who had known his brother and be confronted with painful memories. As a pharmacist, Kaikea's work environment was also affected by his trauma. He found himself becoming easily irritated when customers were misbehaving or acting entitled - behaviors that before would have rolled off his back now sent him spiraling into anxiety. His colleagues began to notice the change in him, commenting on how short-tempered he had become. Kaikea couldn't understand why he was reacting this way. He knew intellectually that the customers weren't a threat, but his body seemed to be reacting before his mind could catch up. He felt constantly tense and ready to react, like he was waiting for another shoe to drop. When memories of Mana's death did surface, Kaikea often felt intense guilt wash over him. He couldn't shake the feeling that he should have done something to prevent it - that somehow, someway, he could have saved his brother. The memories themselves were disjointed and fragmented, like pieces of a puzzle that refused to fit together. Sometimes, when Kaikea did try to recall what happened, he felt completely numb. It was as if the events had occurred to someone else entirely - not the young man who stood behind the pharmacy counter, trying to muster up a smile for his customers. Lately, Kaikea had started noticing that even the smallest things triggered memories of Mana's death. The smell of alcohol wafting from a nearby bar would send him reeling back into grief. He began to wonder if he was going crazy - why these seemingly innocuous things could evoke such intense emotions in him. Kaikea felt like his life had been destroyed by the trauma. He used to love his job, but now it just felt like a monotonous grind. Nothing brought him joy anymore - not even spending time with loved ones or pursuing hobbies he once enjoyed. It was as if the light had gone out of his world. It wasn't until Kaikea's manager sat him down and expressed concern about his behavior that he realized something needed to change. His colleagues were starting to distance themselves from him, and his performance at work was suffering. Kaikea knew he couldn't keep going on like this - but the thought of confronting the pain head-on terrified him. What finally brought Kaikea to seek help was a quiet moment alone in his apartment, when the weight of his grief and anxiety became too much to bear. He looked around at the walls that had once been filled with laughter and memories, now echoing only with silence - and he knew it was time to try and rebuild.
